title: Throw it so fast it never lands
hook: Throw a ball hard enough and it misses the whole planet. How hard is hard enough?

knows: balls fall back to the ground
a faster throw lands further away
doesNotKnow: that an orbit is falling around a curved planet

misconception: Satellites stay up because they escape gravity, or because there is no gravity up there.
objective: The learner can explain that an orbit is a throw so fast that the ground curves away as quickly as the ball falls, at about 7.9 km/s near Earth's surface.

claims.text: With no air, a ball thrown sideways near Earth's surface at about 7.9 km/s circles the planet without landing: circular orbit speed is sqrt(g R) = 7.9 km/s for R = 6371 km.
claims.source: Centripetal acceleration v^2/R equals g: v = sqrt(9.81 x 6.371e6) = 7906 m/s. Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 13 (satellites). From the stage's 10 km peak the circular speed is sqrt(GM/(R+h)) = 7899 m/s, so the 7.9 km/s stop closes the loop.

claims.text: From a 10 km peak with no air, throws at 0.79, 4.0, 7.0, 7.6, 7.8 and 7.85 km/s land about 36, 212, 686, 1,269, 2,245 and 3,209 km away; 7.9 km/s comes back round after about 85 minutes. The speed of every throw is shown after the commit.
claims.source: src/demos/physics/throw-it-fast-enough/model.ts: velocity-Verlet integration of a = -GM r / |r|^3 with GM = g R^2, dt = 1 s, spherical non-rotating Earth. The stage draws these same flights. Loop time 5077 s. · v5 (2026-10-14): unchanged numbers (builder re-ran model.ts with node --experimental-strip-types: 36, 212, 686, 1269, 2245, 3209 km; 7.9 back round at 85 min). The slider now shows each throw's speed; text changed only by the last sentence. | FC pass 26 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Ran model.ts fly() with node --experimental-strip-types (copy in scratchpad fc26-b1): 0.79, 4.0, 7.0, 7.6, 7.8, 7.85 km/s land at 36, 212, 686, 1,269, 2,245, 3,209 km; 7.9 does not land, back round at 5,077 s = 84.6 min, readout rounds to 85. Slider format prints kms(v) whenever unlocked.

claims.text: The lesson ignores air and Earth's spin, treats Earth as a sphere, and exaggerates heights 40 times on the stage.
claims.source: Stated on stage ('No air. 10 km peak. Heights x40.') and in the reveal. Real air at 10 km would stop such a throw; the mountain follows Newton's thought experiment (Principia, A Treatise of the System of the World, 1728).

claims.text: The ISS orbits at about 7.7 km/s, about 400 km up; slower than 7.9 km/s because gravity is weaker at that height.
claims.source: NASA, International Space Station facts and figures: altitude about 400 km, speed about 17,500 mph (7.8 km/s, rounded). Circular speed at 400 km: sqrt(GM / 6771 km) = 7.67 km/s with GM = g R^2.

claims.text: In its first minute every throw from 7.0 to 7.9 km/s falls 17.6 km below the straight sideways line from the peak, while the ground curves away below that line by 13.9 km (7.0 km/s), 16.3 km (7.6), 17.2 km (7.8), 17.4 km (7.85) and 17.6 km (7.9): at 7.9 km/s the ground curves away as fast as the ball falls. The 0.79 and 4.0 km/s throws land within the first minute. The reveal says 'your {fastest landing} and 7.9 km/s throws both fell 17.6 km' only when the fastest landing the learner moved to is 7.0 km/s or faster (it has a first-minute record with the same 17.6 km fall); if it is 0.79 or 4.0 km/s it says 'your 7.9 km/s throw fell 17.6 km'.
claims.source: fly() in model.ts records the ball at t = 60 s; fell = lineHeight(angle) - height, groundAway = lineHeight(angle) - 10 km, where lineHeight is the height of the straight sideways line from the peak ((R+P)/cos(angle) - R). Run with node: fell 17.6 km for 7.0 to 7.9 km/s (cf. g t^2 / 2 = 17.66 km); groundAway 13.9, 16.3, 17.2, 17.4, 17.6 km. 0.79 and 4.0 km/s land at about 36 and 212 km, before 60 s. The reveal quotes the fastest landing throw the learner moved to, and the 85-minute lap is shown on the Lands readout. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Ran model.ts fly() in node (strip-types): at t = 60 s fell = 17.638-17.643 km (km1 -> 17.6) for 7.0-7.9 km/s; groundAway 13.86, 16.33, 17.20, 17.42, 17.65 km -> 13.9, 16.3, 17.2, 17.4, 17.6; 0.79 and 4.0 km/s land at t = 46 s and 53 s (36 and 212 km), so minute = null for them ('Landed within the first minute.'). Cross-check: g(R/(R+P))^2 t^2/2 = 17.60 km. · v5 (2026-10-14): scoped to 7.0-7.9 km/s because the new 9.0 km/s stop falls 17.7 km in its first minute (model.ts, builder node run). Needs re-check. | FC pass 26 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): DISPUTED (the reveal sentence on a reachable branch). Numbers hold: at t = 60 s fell 17.638-17.643 km (17.6) for 7.0-7.9 km/s; groundAway 13.86, 16.33, 17.20, 17.42, 17.65 km; 0.79 and 4.0 land at 46 s and 53 s. But the reveal prints 'your {near} and 7.9 km/s throws both fell 17.6 km' with near = fastest landing tried, and fell is taken from the 7.9 flight only. The slider is a native range: Home (or a track click) jumps from 7.8 to 0.79 (lands: 'landed'), then a track click on 7.9 ('loop') opens the reveal with near = 0.79 km/s, which reads 'your 0.79 km/s and 7.9 km/s throws both fell 17.6 km below the dashed straight line' - false (that throw hit the ground at 46 s, about 10 km below the line). Same for 4.0 km/s. Fix (demo-builder): when near.minute is null, drop near from that sentence (e.g. 'your 7.9 km/s throw fell 17.6 km ...'), or print near.minute.fell for near. | v6 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, W-248): reveal sentence now conditional: names the fastest landing only when near.minute exists and km1(near.minute.fell) equals km1(loop.minute.fell); otherwise only the 7.9 km/s throw. Numbers unchanged. Needs re-check.

claims.text: Faster than 7.9 km/s also never lands: at 9.0 km/s the ball swings far out and comes back round after about 144 minutes (in its first minute it falls 17.7 km below the straight line while the ground curves away 22.9 km); at 79 km/s it flies off into space ('never: escapes').
claims.source: model.ts fly(9000) and fly(79000), builder node run 2026-10-14: 9.0 km/s does not land, back round at t = 144 min, minute fell 17.7 km, groundAway 22.9 km; 79 km/s has v^2/2 - GM/r > 0 at the throw (escape speed from the peak sqrt(2GM/(R + 10 km)) = 11.17 km/s), integration stopped at 4 R_E. Builder statement, not self-verified. | FC pass 26 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own run of fly(9000): lands false, escapes false, back round at 8,630 s (143.8 min, readout 144), minute fell 17.650 km (17.7), groundAway 22.892 km (22.9), peak height about 5,429 km above ground (swings far out). fly(79000): escapes (v^2/2 - GM/r > 0; escape speed from the peak sqrt(2GM/(R+10 km)) = 11.17 km/s), stopped at t = 315 s, 19,158 km up (> 4 R_E from centre). Stage: caption 'First minute: fell 17.7 km ...; the ground curved away 22.9 km.' at 9.0, 'Too fast to stay' and Lands 'never: escapes' at 79.

recall.question: Why does the International Space Station not fall to the ground?
options: There is no gravity at its height
It is falling, but moving sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it
Its engines keep pushing it up
recall.why: An orbit is free fall with enough sideways speed (about 7.7 km/s at 400 km) that the curved surface drops away as fast as the station falls.
